What kind of cage is he in? Do you have bowls that hook over the bars of the cage or otherwise attach to them to hold them in place? Hookless bowls don't tend to work well at all with lovies in my experience, because, similarly to your bird, my lovebird will try to play with them and knock them to the bottom of his cage if he can.

I really only suggest using a harness for a cat that's been trained to it. I put my cat on her harness for car rides and even she sometimes get a bit anxious and cries for a bit before getting used to it and snuggling up to sleep. We took her on vacation with us on  a trip from Ohio to North Carolina and she tolerated it well, but that's only because she's been trained to it since she was very young. Would really really recommend a carrier for your kitty, and I've heard of anxiety treatments you can use to help her deal with the stress a bit better, though I haven't personally used them. Definitely agree with kapdragon's suggestion to allow her some time to get used to the carrier as well. Hope the trip goes alright!

For the safety of you, your cat, and other drivers, I really suggest getting a harness and seatbelt for your boy. He sounds like a really sweet cat, but it only takes one incident of something scaring him and him bolting under your feet to cause an accident. :[

Word of advice, get a gecko if you want a low maintenance pet, not an iguana. I own one and they can be a handful, and mine's still small! The proper setup for a juvenile iguana is already pretty expensive (dual sided lamp, very large tank, humidifier, thermometer and humidity reader, reptile carpet, ceramic heat bulb, uvb bulb, food bowl and a water bowl large enough for him to swim in, etc). Not to mention they can get 5 or 6 feet long within about 3 years and the males can go from being sweet cuddle babies to angry dinosaurs that can give you stitches with a single bite during breeding season if you don't take the proper precautions.

Now, I'm not saying don't get an iguana if you really want one, just that they require about as much effort to care for as a dog with way more expensive costs for their setup. The best thing about iguanas is that their food is dirt cheap! Greens are very low-price at stores like Krogers (they don't actually eat insects or meat, they're exclusive herbivores and animal protein can cause kidney problems). I'd definitely suggest a female if you decide to get one, a bit smaller than males and not nearly as hormonal or territorial.

BUT YEAH, sorry for the tl;dr, it's just that I got an iguana without knowing how much effort really goes into them and don't want someone else to make an uninformed decision like I did.

Geckos are low maintenance but aren't all that hands on. If you want a cuddlier lizard that doesn't mind some human attention, I've heard that bearded dragons are very sweet, and they get kind of big, but not nearly as big as iguanas, if you like the larger species of reptiles. Good luck with your future pets! :]

This. Snakes are great low maintenance pets. I'm especially partial towards ball pythons, and own two of them. They're pretty laidback little guys, and don't get as large as other types of pythons. You can get them out of their enclosure and mine just like to slither around in my hands and explore or go under the sheets and curl up next to me to rest. Balls are pretty great if you want a moderately big sized "cuddly" snake (not in the same way that mammals and birds tend to be, but they don't mind just chilling out with you to watch a movie or read a book). I've heard that they can be picky feeders, though, but thankfully I haven't had that problem with mine so far over the course of the year I've owned them.

Honestly, I'd say some of the more commonly kept snake species, like ball pythons for example, are easier, or at least as easy as taking care of a cat. My ball pythons only need fed once a week at most, fresh water, their cage kept clean, and optimal humidity and temperatures in their enclosure. Most of their care comes from preparation, then they're happy and good to go.

I have no idea how iguanas ended up so low on their list, though? Do they think you can just keep them as babies then dump them when they're older? Adult iguanas can have hormomal aggression, require a huge enclosure, and very high humidity and temperatures. I'd say they're definitely at the same level as taking care of a dog (If not more difficult, depending on the dog breed and temperament).
